description: How Roman cities were planned — the grid, the forum, and life in Rome, Ostia and Pompeii.
content_html:
Why Did Rome Build Cities?

When Rome conquered new territory, it did not simply station soldiers and move on. It built cities. Across the empire, from Britain to Syria, Roman towns followed recognisable patterns: wide streets laid out on a grid, a central forum for business and politics, public baths, temples, markets and amphitheatres. This consistency was not an accident. The Romans understood that a well-planned city reinforced Roman identity, encouraged commerce, and projected the power of the empire onto a conquered landscape. Understanding the design of a Roman city is therefore not just about architecture — it is about understanding how Rome controlled and civilised its world.

The Grid Plan

Most Roman towns were laid out on a grid plan. Two main roads formed the backbone: the cardo ran north to south and the decumanus ran east to west. They crossed at the heart of the town, usually at or near the forum. Secondary streets branched off these two main arteries, dividing the town into rectangular blocks called insulae (islands). This plan made it easy to navigate, to administer, and to expand a city in an orderly way.

Pavements lined the main streets, raised above the road surface so that pedestrians were protected from wheeled traffic and from the mud and waste that accumulated in the roadway. In Pompeii, wide stepping stones allowed people to cross from one pavement to another without descending to road level. The gaps between the stepping stones were spaced to allow cart wheels to pass through. This detail, preserved at Pompeii, tells us a great deal about the volume and type of traffic on Roman streets and the practical solutions Romans devised to manage it.

Key Fact

The Roman town grid was organised around the cardo (north–south) and the decumanus (east–west). They crossed near the forum, the civic and commercial heart of the city. This grid plan was used across the empire, from Pompeii in Italy to Timgad in North Africa.

Water Supply and Sanitation

No Roman city functioned without water. Aqueducts brought fresh water into the city from springs sometimes many kilometres away. At Pompeii, the main aqueduct fed a high-pressure water tower called a castellum aquae, from which lead and terracotta pipes distributed water to public fountains, the baths, and wealthy private houses. Most ordinary residents collected their water from the public fountains placed at regular intervals along the streets; fresh water was never more than a short walk away. Inscriptions on the water tower at Pompeii suggest that the system was carefully maintained and that officials were responsible for its upkeep.

Drainage was equally important. Deep stone-lined sewers ran beneath the streets, carrying waste water away from fountains, baths and latrines. The great Cloaca Maxima (Great Sewer) at Rome was an engineering marvel that drained the low-lying area of the Forum Romanum and discharged into the Tiber. Its construction was attributed in ancient tradition to the early kings of Rome, and it continued to function throughout the imperial period.

The Forum

The forum was the beating heart of any Roman city. At Pompeii, the main forum took the form of a large rectangular open space, measuring roughly 38 by 157 metres, surrounded on three sides by a two-storey colonnade. This colonnaded walkway provided shade for the merchants, lawyers and citizens who gathered there daily. At the north end of the forum stood the Temple of Jupiter, the most important religious building in the city, its raised podium dominating the space. On the other sides stood civic buildings: the basilica (a large covered hall for legal and commercial business), the comitium (an assembly room), and offices for the elected magistrates who governed the town.

The forum was not merely practical. It was a statement of Roman values. By placing the temple of the chief god at its head, surrounded by the buildings of law and government, the Romans visually demonstrated that their civic life was underpinned by divine authority. Statues of emperors and local benefactors stood throughout the space, reminding every visitor of the hierarchy of power that made their ordered city possible.

Pompeii and Herculaneum were buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79, preserving streets, buildings and even food in extraordinary detail. This makes them our richest sources for everyday Roman town life. Pompeii was a medium-sized town of perhaps 12,000 people; Herculaneum was smaller but its wealthier character is clear from the quality of its surviving houses and wall paintings. Both towns demonstrate the grid plan, the forum complex, and the full range of amenities — baths, theatres, food stalls, temples and private homes — that characterised a typical Roman city.

Ostia, the port of Rome, offers a different perspective. Because Ostia continued to be occupied and altered after the eruption that preserved Pompeii, it shows how a Roman city evolved over time. At Ostia the famous Insula of Diana — a multi-storey apartment block — illustrates how the city housed its growing population by building upwards. Taken together, Pompeii, Herculaneum and Ostia provide complementary evidence for Roman urban life at different social levels and different stages of development.

Streets, Shops and the Busy City

Roman streets were not quiet. The poet Juvenal, writing in the late first or early second century AD, painted a vivid picture of the dangers of navigating Rome at night: carts rumbling past, buckets of waste thrown from upper-storey windows, and the constant roar of the city. His Satire 3 describes a man who cannot sleep for the noise and who walks in fear of collapsing buildings. While Juvenal exaggerated for satirical effect, his complaints reflect genuine conditions. In Rome, wheeled traffic was banned from the city centre during daylight hours to ease congestion, so deliveries were made at night, adding to the noise.

The ground floors of buildings lining Roman streets were typically given over to shops and workshops. At Pompeii, hundreds of small commercial premises — identifiable by their wide doorways designed to allow goods and customers easy access — opened directly onto the street. Many were thermopolia: food and drink stalls with stone counters set with large ceramic jars, from which vendors served warm food to customers who had no cooking facilities at home. The inscriptions and painted notices preserved on Pompeii’s walls also reveal an active culture of political campaigning, advertising and personal messages, bringing the city to life in a way no other Roman site can match.

Key Fact

Roman towns were full of commercial activity. The thermopolia (hot food stalls) at Pompeii show that many residents ate street food rather than cooking at home. Around 80 thermopolia have been identified in Pompeii alone, suggesting that not having a kitchen was normal for ordinary city dwellers.

It is easy to think of “Roman city life” as meaning only the city of Rome itself. But the Roman empire was covered in cities, many of them following similar plans and containing similar buildings. Pompeii, Herculaneum and Ostia are all Italian towns, not Rome itself. This matters because they give us evidence for what life was like in a typical medium-sized Roman city, rather than in the extraordinary capital. When you use Pompeii as evidence, you should note that it was a prosperous but unremarkable town — not an imperial showpiece — and that this actually makes it more useful as evidence for ordinary Roman life.
exam_tip_html: The command word Describe asks you to say what is there — give accurate details about appearance, layout or features. For a source question on town planning (for example, a view of the Pompeii forum or a street with stepping stones), pick out specific details from the source and connect them to your knowledge. A common mistake is to write generally about “Roman cities” without anchoring your answer to the named site (Pompeii, Ostia, Herculaneum or Rome) that the question is asking about. Always name your site and say what the specific evidence reveals.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Roman cities were laid out on a grid plan centred on the cardo and decumanus, which crossed at the forum — the civic, commercial and religious heart of the city.
  • Pompeii, Herculaneum and Ostia give us different but complementary evidence: Pompeii’s eruption-preserved streets reveal everyday commercial life; Ostia’s apartment blocks show how cities housed their growing populations.
  • Roman city streets were busy and noisy; Juvenal’s Satire 3 describes their dangers with satirical exaggeration, while Pompeii’s stepping stones and thermopolia provide physical evidence of how Romans navigated and fed themselves in the city.

practice_questions.text: Name one of the two main roads in a Roman town grid plan.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: cardo OR decumanus (either name accepted).

practice_questions.text: Describe what the forum of Pompeii looked like and how it was used.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for up to three accurate details: e.g. large open rectangular space / surrounded by a two-storey colonnade / Temple of Jupiter at the north end / basilica and magistrates' offices on the sides / statues of emperors and benefactors / centre for civic, commercial and religious life. No marks for vague generalities; each point needs a specific feature.

practice_questions.text: Read the following passage, which paraphrases Juvenal's Satire 3. In it, a man describes the miseries of living in Rome: the constant rumble of carts at night, the fear of falling masonry from badly built upper storeys, and buckets of waste hurled from windows above. What does this source tell us about life in a Roman city? What are its limitations as evidence?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses specific details from the source (carts at night, falling masonry, waste from windows) and connects each to knowledge of Roman city conditions (ban on daytime wheeled traffic, poorly built insulae, lack of sanitation). Evaluates the source's limitations with precision — Juvenal is a satirist writing for a wealthy audience; he exaggerates for comic effect and represents only one viewpoint. Reaches a supported judgement about how useful the source is.
Secure: Uses at least two details from the source and links them to knowledge. Identifies at least one limitation (satire / exaggeration / limited viewpoint) with some explanation.
Developing: Picks out a detail or two and makes a general comment about limitations without full development.
Emerging: Paraphrases the source or makes very general points about Roman city life without engaging with the text.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the grid plan was a useful design for Roman cities.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a reason; 1 mark for explaining it. Up to two explained reasons for full marks. E.g.: Easy navigation (1) — a regular street pattern meant both residents and newcomers could find their way without getting lost, making trade and administration more efficient (1). Ease of expansion (1) — new blocks could simply be added to the existing grid, allowing the city to grow in an orderly way (1). Easy administration (1) — the regular layout made it simple to identify properties, collect taxes and maintain public buildings (1). Any two well-explained reasons score full marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful are Pompeii and Herculaneum as evidence for everyday life in Roman cities? Use sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues with precision, using named sources (thermopolia, stepping stones, forum colonnade, inscriptions, Insula of Diana at Ostia for comparison). Evaluates both the value of the evidence (exceptional preservation, wide range of building types, commercial and domestic detail) and its limits (both are frozen in AD 79; both are Italian towns, not the capital; Pompeii may not represent the poorest Romans). Reaches a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Uses two or more named examples from Pompeii or Herculaneum and makes a clear argument about usefulness, with at least one evaluative point.
Developing: Describes what Pompeii reveals but does not evaluate; argument is one-sided or unsupported.
Emerging: General statements about Pompeii without named evidence.

practice_questions.text: How far do the physical remains of Pompeii give us a complete picture of Roman city life? In your answer, refer to both the evidence and its limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument using a range of named sources (e.g. thermopolia, forum layout, stepping stones, wall-paintings, graffiti inscriptions, water tower/castellum aquae). Considers both strength of evidence (extraordinary preservation; wide range of building types; evidence from both wealthy and ordinary households) and limitations (single moment in time — AD 79; not the capital; limited evidence for the very poorest; bias towards surviving stone buildings). Reaches a supported judgement about how complete the picture is, perhaps noting that Ostia or literary sources like Juvenal fill some of the gaps.
Secure: Clear argument using several named examples; evaluates both strength and limitation; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Describes the evidence but does not evaluate it critically; argument is largely one-sided.
Emerging: General descriptive points about Pompeii without use of specific named evidence.

knowledge_checks.q: Which road in the Roman town grid plan ran north to south?
What is a thermopolium in a Roman city?
options: A hot food and drink stall

knowledge_checks.q: The two main roads of a Roman town met at the _____, the civic and commercial heart of the city.
The satirist _____ described the dangers of Roman city streets in Satire 3, including collapsing buildings and noise.
Match each Roman town to the feature it best illustrates.
right: Grid streets, forum and thermopolia preserved by Vesuvius
Multi-storey apartment blocks showing how populations were housed
Smaller, wealthier town with fine wall paintings also buried by Vesuvius

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two main roads in a Roman town grid plan called?
Where did the cardo and decumanus usually cross in a Roman town?
flashcard_questions.a: At the forum, the civic and commercial heart of the city.
A Roman hot food and drink stall with a stone counter set with ceramic jars.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was wheeled traffic banned from central Rome during daylight hours?
flashcard_questions.a: To ease congestion; deliveries were made at night instead.

flashcard_questions.q: What caused Pompeii and Herculaneum to be so well preserved?
flashcard_questions.a: They were buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the stepping stones evidence at Pompeii tell us?
flashcard_questions.a: That streets were wet and dirty, and that wheeled cart traffic was common.

flashcard_questions.q: What was an aqueduct used for in a Roman city?
flashcard_questions.a: Carrying fresh water from distant springs into the city.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Roman author described the miseries of city life in Satire 3?
What building type at Ostia shows how Roman cities housed growing populations?
flashcard_questions.a: The multi-storey insula apartment block, e.g. the Insula of Diana.

flashcard_questions.q: What stood at the north end of the Pompeii forum?
flashcard_questions.a: The Temple of Jupiter, the most important religious building in the city.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one limitation of using Pompeii as evidence for Roman city life.
flashcard_questions.a: It is frozen at one moment (AD 79) and is not the capital, so may not represent Rome itself.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Latin word 'forum' refer to in a Roman city?
flashcard_questions.a: The central open square of a Roman city; the focus of public civic and religious life.

glossary_terms.definition: A regular street layout based on two main roads crossing at right angles, dividing the town into rectangular blocks.
The main north-south street of a Roman town, forming one of the two principal axes of the grid plan.
The main east-west road of a Roman town, crossing the cardo at or near the forum.
The open central square of a Roman city, serving as the focus of civic, commercial and religious life.
A Roman structure, often raised on arches, that carried a channel of fresh water from distant springs into a town.
A Roman street-level food and drink shop, identifiable by its stone counter set with large ceramic jars for serving hot food.
